Staged cascade: state-blocked bulk, then an unblocked residual sweep

Source: R/match.R
pf_staged_passes.Rd

The production shape for the full file. pf_default_passes() blocks nothing geographically, which is the right instrument for measuring geographic mismatch but is unaffordable at 12.5M grants: its cross-state token pass compares against all 1.9M BMF records and accounts for 96% of the runtime.

Usage

pf_staged_passes(
  sweep = c("lean", "full", "none"),
  concat = TRUE,
  max_ref_freq_state = 25000,
  min_pair_idf_state = 8,
  max_ref_freq_any = 5000,
  min_pair_idf_any = 8
)

Arguments

sweep

How much of the unblocked residual sweep to run (see above).

concat

Include the adjacent-token compound pass B2, which recovers de-spacing differences (STEP FORWARD vs STEPFORWARD). Measured cost on 5,000 grants: 223,151 candidates — 46% of the whole lean cascade — for 48 YES matches. Keep it when recall matters more than runtime; drop it for a fast first pass over the full file, since most of what it finds degrades to MAYBE rather than disappearing.

max_ref_freq_state, min_pair_idf_state

Token pruning inside a state.

max_ref_freq_any, min_pair_idf_any

Token pruning for the unblocked sweep, tighter because the pool is the whole BMF.

Value

A list of pass specifications for npmatch::np_cascade().

Details

This cascade splits into three stages, tightest first. Because npmatch::np_cascade() prunes only queries that reached YES, everything unresolved — including every MAYBE — falls through to the next stage, so blocking early costs recall only for records the later stages also miss.

Stage A — state-blocked exact (very cheap)

Exact name against exact ZIP5, then against state, then the name/DBA cross-products within state. ZIP5 implies state, so the first pass needs no separate state key.

Stage B — state-blocked token (moderate)

Shared distinctive name token within state, then the same with adjacent-token compounds. This is where the bulk of the fuzzy work happens, against ~1/15th of the reference rather than all of it.

Stage C — unblocked residual sweep (expensive, small N)

Only the queries still unresolved reach here. This is what makes the state block safe: it recovers the cases state blocking cannot see — a 990-PF state field that is simply wrong (six of the ten cross-state YES matches in the benchmark had matching city and ZIP but a wrong state code), a national headquarters address in the BMF against a local grantee address, a lockbox, and every record whose state is missing entirely (a blocked pass drops those, since .np_bykey() treats an incomplete key as invalid).

Choosing sweep

Measured on 5,000 grants, the unblocked token sweep (C3) generated 686,380 candidate pairs — 59% of the entire run — and produced zero additional YES matches; its only product is MAYBE candidates for adjudication. The four YES matches stage C did contribute all came from the cheap exact pass C1, and three of those four are the known cross-state false positives (UNBOUND MO->KS, FIRST PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IA->NC, PATTERSON VOLUNTEER FIRE DEPARTMENT LA->NC) — common names matched in another state with no address corroboration.

The cross-state cases that are genuine — a 990-PF state field simply typed wrong, with city and ZIP both correct — never needed an unblocked sweep at all: pass A1 blocks on name + ZIP5 and deliberately carries no state key, so it catches them at a fraction of the cost.

  • "lean" (default) — stages A and B plus the cheap exact cross-state passes. Same YES set, roughly half the candidates.

  • "full" — adds the unblocked token sweep. Use when maximising the adjudication queue matters more than runtime.

  • "none" — state-blocked only. Fastest; gives up the state-typo recovery that A1 cannot reach (a wrong state and a wrong ZIP).
